home.meta.title: Ocy — a calm break reminder for your eyes
home.meta.description: A calm break reminder for Windows to ease eye strain. Short eye exercises every few minutes, a real hourly break, no account, works offline. Get it on the Microsoft Store.

home.hero.heading: A calm break reminder for your eyes
home.hero.sub: Short eye exercises every few minutes, a real break every hour, and quiet when you need focus.

home.works.2.title: You step away

home.exercises.heading: Twelve tiny exercises
home.exercises.sub: Hand-drawn style, a few frames each, like a flip book.
home.exercises.why.blink: Screens make us blink less. Slow, full blinks spread fresh tears across your eyes.
home.exercises.why.look-left-right: A change from holding your eyes in one fixed position.
home.exercises.why.look-up-down: Uses the up-and-down range your eyes hardly touch while reading a screen.
home.exercises.why.roll: Slow circles take your eyes through their full range, then let them rest.
home.exercises.why.close-tight: A gentle squeeze and release relaxes the muscles around your eyes.
home.exercises.why.near-far: Changing focus gives your eyes a break from screen distance.
home.exercises.why.window-far: Looking far away lets your eyes relax from close-up focus.
home.exercises.why.figure-eight: A slow, smooth path keeps your eyes moving without strain.
home.exercises.why.palming: A warm, dark moment with no screen light, for tired eyes.
home.exercises.why.stretch-arms: Opens your chest and shoulders after leaning toward a screen.
home.exercises.why.neck-shoulders: Eases the tension that builds in your neck and shoulders while you sit.
home.exercises.why.stand-walk: A few steps get you moving and change your posture.

home.faq.heading: Questions
home.faq.artAria: Ocy looking up, with question marks around its head
home.faq.1.q: Is Ocy an alternative to EyeLeo?
home.faq.1.a: Yes. If you used EyeLeo, which hasn’t been updated in years, Ocy covers the same daily routine: short eye exercises, regular long breaks and quiet during fullscreen work. It also shows breaks on the monitor you are using, counts time away as rest, and runs on Windows today, with macOS and Linux planned. Ocy is an independent project, and its code, exercises and art are all original.
home.faq.2.a: Yes. Ocy comes from the Microsoft Store, which checks every app before it is listed. It needs no account and sends nothing unless you say yes to the optional usage stats or to sending a crash report.
home.faq.2.aCrashOnly: Yes. Ocy comes from the Microsoft Store, which checks every app before it is listed. It needs no account and sends nothing unless you agree to send a crash report.
home.faq.3.q: How do I start it with Windows, or remove it?
home.faq.3.a: Turn on {setting} in Settings. To remove Ocy, uninstall it from Windows Settings → Apps. Its settings stay in {appdata}; delete that folder too if you want them gone.
home.faq.4.a: Short break every 25 min, for 15 s. Long break every 60 min, for 5 min. Warning 60 s before a long break. Postpone 3 min, up to 3 times. You count as away after 2 min without input. All of it is adjustable in Settings.
home.faq.4.tableNote: All of it is adjustable in Settings, without a restart.
home.faq.4.row1.label: Short break
home.faq.4.row2.label: Long break
home.faq.4.row3.label: Warning before a long break
home.faq.4.row4.label: Postpone
home.faq.4.row5.label: You count as away after
home.faq.5.q: Does it slow my PC down?
home.faq.5.a: No. Ocy uses about 3.7 MB of memory while it waits and about 5–6 MB during a break. It checks in about six times a minute, and the whole app is one 12 MB file.
home.faq.6.q: Can I use a screen reader?
home.faq.6.a: Yes. Ocy supports Windows UI Automation, so Narrator can read it. Breaks never steal focus from what you are doing.
home.faq.7.a: Ocy is a one-time purchase on the Microsoft Store, with a 15-day free trial first. No subscription and no ads.
home.faq.8.a: No. Ocy works fully offline. If you turn on the optional usage stats or agree to send a crash report, they are sent when you're online.
home.faq.8.aCrashOnly: No. Ocy works fully offline. If you agree to send a crash report, it is sent the next time you're online.
home.faq.9.q: Will it interrupt my game, video call or presentation?
home.faq.9.a: Presentations and fullscreen videos hold breaks until you’re done. In games, breaks come as a small card in a calm moment, never mid-fight, and “Not during this game” keeps any game silent. Detecting calls in windowed apps is on the roadmap.
home.faq.10.q: Can I make it stricter or gentler?
home.faq.10.a: Yes. Change how often breaks come and how long they last, or turn off postponing and skipping with strict mode.
home.faq.11.a: No. Ocy is a habit tool. If your eyes hurt or your vision changes, see an eye-care professional.
privacy.meta.title: Privacy — Ocy
privacy.meta.description: Ocy works offline, needs no account and keeps its files on your PC. Anonymous usage stats are sent only if you turn them on.
privacy.heading: Privacy
privacy.sub: What Ocy keeps on your PC, and what it can send if you say yes.
privacy.lede: Ocy needs no account and works without the internet. There are no ads and no tracking of what you do on your PC. Ocy can send two things, and only if you say yes: an anonymous daily summary of its break counts and settings, and a crash report if it ever closes unexpectedly.
privacy.usage.heading: Anonymous usage stats (optional)
privacy.stored.heading: What is stored on your PC
privacy.stored.intro: Ocy keeps a few small files in {appdata}:
privacy.stored.state: break timers, so a restart continues where you left off
privacy.stored.errors: a small error log, at most 256 KB, rotated
privacy.stored.usage: only while usage stats are on: the random ID and the last day sent
privacy.stored.outro: These files stay on your PC. Only the optional reports described on this page are ever sent, and only if you say yes. To remove the files, quit Ocy from the tray and delete that folder.
privacy.activity.heading: How activity is checked
privacy.activity.body: To count active screen time and pause during fullscreen apps, Ocy checks idle time, lock and sleep session events, and fullscreen state locally on your PC. None of it is recorded or sent anywhere.
privacy.website.heading: This website
privacy.website.body: This site is static HTML hosted on GitHub Pages. It sets no cookies, runs no analytics, and makes zero external requests — no third-party fonts, CDNs or embeds.
privacy.ai.heading: Development & generative AI disclosure
privacy.ai.body1: Ocy is designed, directed and maintained by damt.xyz with extensive use of generative AI tools, from start to finish: most of the application code and tests, the documentation, the translations, this website, the store listing and other marketing materials, and ongoing maintenance.
privacy.ai.body2: This applies only to how Ocy is made and marketed. When you run Ocy, no AI model is involved.
privacy.ai.body3: Throughout, a real person steers the work and decides what is released.
privacy.opensource.heading: Open source
privacy.opensource.body: Ocy is licensed under AGPL-3.0. You can inspect the full source code on {github} or {homeLink}.

privacy.usage.plain: If you say yes, Ocy sends us one short note a day: how many breaks you took or skipped, and how your breaks are set up. That's all. It never includes your name, your files, what you do on your PC, or which programs or games you use. It's off until you turn it on, and you can turn it off, or ask us to delete what was sent, at any time. We use it only to make Ocy better, and we never sell it or use it for ads.
privacy.usage.detailsIntro: Everything below is exactly what Ocy sends. Nothing else is included.
privacy.usage.eventsIntro: Ocy sends two kinds of messages, called events:
privacy.usage.eventEnabled: {name}: sent once, right after you say yes.
privacy.usage.eventDaily: {name}: one for each full day after the day you said yes, sent once that day is over. It never covers the day you said yes or the current day, and after a long pause Ocy sends at most the last 14 days.
privacy.usage.table.caption: Every field in an event
privacy.usage.f.distinctId: the random ID created on your PC when you said yes
privacy.usage.f.uuid: the message's own ID, made from the random ID and the date, so a message sent twice is counted once
privacy.usage.f.timestamp: the day the message is about, always at 12:00 UTC, so no time of day is sent
privacy.usage.f.personProfile: tells PostHog not to build a profile of anyone
privacy.usage.f.geoip: tells PostHog not to look up a location
privacy.usage.f.lib: says the message comes from Ocy
privacy.usage.f.platform: the operating system: Windows, Linux or macOS
privacy.usage.f.osVersion: the system version number (on Linux only the kernel version, such as 6.8)
privacy.usage.f.channel: where Ocy came from: the Microsoft Store, GitHub, Flathub, or the Linux or macOS download
privacy.usage.f.license: the Store license: trial, full, trial ended, none (not from the Store) or unknown
privacy.usage.f.uiLanguage: the language Ocy is shown in
privacy.usage.f.locale: your system's language and region setting
privacy.usage.f.shortCounts: short breaks taken and skipped that day
privacy.usage.f.longCounts: long breaks taken, skipped and postponed that day
privacy.usage.f.absences: times you were away long enough to count as a long break
privacy.usage.f.activeMinutes: minutes you were active at the screen that day
privacy.usage.f.preset: your break preset: gentle, balanced, focused or custom
privacy.usage.f.shortSettings: your short-break settings: on or off, how often (minutes) and how long (seconds)
privacy.usage.f.longSettings: your long-break settings: on or off, how often (minutes) and how long (minutes)
privacy.usage.f.switches: whether each of these settings is on or off
privacy.usage.f.gamesMode: how breaks behave in games: gentle or hold
privacy.usage.enabledNote: {name} carries only the first 13 fields, up to {last}: no counts and no settings.
privacy.usage.neverBody: Your name or account details, file or folder paths, window titles, the programs or games you use (not even your list of silent games), your IP address or your location.
privacy.usage.howBody: Over an encrypted HTTPS connection to {host}, about a minute after Ocy starts, then at most once an hour until the day's summary has been accepted. If you're offline, it waits. Nothing older than 14 days is kept waiting.
privacy.usage.keyNote: Each message also carries Ocy's project key. It is a public, send-only key: it can add messages but cannot read any data.
privacy.usage.whereHeading: Where it goes and who sees it
privacy.usage.whereBody: PostHog, an analytics service, stores the messages in its EU region and processes them on our behalf. Every connection has an IP address; PostHog is set to discard it instead of storing it, and not to look up a location. The data is kept for up to 2 years, then deleted automatically. Only damt.xyz, the developer of Ocy, can see it. It is never sold and never shared for advertising.
privacy.usage.pcBody: While sharing is on, Ocy keeps {file} in {appdata}. It holds the random ID ({installId}), the day you said yes ({optedInDate}), the last day sent ({lastSentDate}), whether the first message was sent ({enabledEventSent}) and the file's format version ({schemaVersion}). Turning sharing off deletes the file.
privacy.usage.rightsBody: We process this data only with your consent, and you can withdraw it at any time by turning the switch off. You can ask what we hold for your anonymous ID, ask us to delete it, and complain to your data protection authority. Contact: {support}
privacy.usage.stopBody: In Ocy, open {settings} → {general} and turn off {switch}. Nothing more is sent, and the random ID is deleted from your PC.
privacy.usage.deleteTitle: Delete what was sent, or ask a question
privacy.usage.deleteBody: Email {support} with your anonymous ID. We delete the data within about 4 weeks: PostHog removes event data in weekly batches, and its backups expire about 2 weeks after that.
privacy.usage.idWhere: Your anonymous ID is the {installId} value in {file} in {appdata}. You can open that file with Notepad.
privacy.usage.firstTitle: Ask before you turn it off
privacy.usage.firstBody: Once the ID is deleted from your PC, the data can no longer be linked to you, not even by us. So if you want it deleted, send your request before you turn sharing off.
home.faq.12.a: Only if you turn on the optional anonymous usage stats. Then Ocy sends one short summary a day of your break counts and settings, never anything about you or what you do on your PC. {link} lists every detail.
home.faq.12.aCrashOnly: No. The only thing Ocy can send is a crash report if it ever closes unexpectedly, and only if you say yes. {link} lists every detail.
privacy.ledeCrashOnly: Ocy needs no account and works without the internet. There are no ads and no tracking of what you do on your PC. The only thing Ocy can send is a crash report if it ever closes unexpectedly, and only if you say yes.
privacy.crash.heading: Crash reports (optional)
privacy.crash.plain: If Ocy ever closes unexpectedly, it saves a short crash report on your PC. The next time Ocy starts, it asks whether to send it. The report says what went wrong and where in Ocy's code, plus Ocy's version and your system version. Nothing personal is in it: no names, no files or folders from your PC, nothing about what you do. You can read the exact report before sending it, choose to always send or never send, and change your mind at any time in Settings. We use crash reports only to fix bugs.
privacy.crash.step1: Ocy crashes: an error in its own code or, on Windows, a deeper system-level crash.
privacy.crash.step2: Ocy saves a report in {folder}, one small file per crash, after removing anything personal. If you chose {never}, it saves nothing.
privacy.crash.step3: About three seconds after Ocy next starts, a small card appears in the corner. It never takes the focus away from what you're doing and waits until no break is on screen. {see} shows the exact text that would be sent, with the report ID and a button to copy it.
privacy.crash.step4: {send} sends the report and {dontSend} deletes it. Tick {dontAsk} to make your choice stick: after {send}, later reports are sent without the card; after {dontSend}, Ocy never asks and never sends. Closing the card keeps the report and asks again next time.
privacy.crash.step5: With {always}, reports are sent in the background without the card, at most 5 a day.
privacy.crash.step6: Once a report has been sent or declined, its file is deleted from your PC.
privacy.crash.eventIntro: Each report is sent as one event called {name}. These are its fields; nothing else is included.
privacy.crash.table.caption: Every field in a crash report
privacy.crash.f.reportId: the report ID: a random ID made for this one report. It is not the usage-stats ID, so crash reports can't be linked to the usage stats or to each other
privacy.crash.f.personProfile: tells PostHog not to build a profile of anyone
privacy.crash.f.geoip: tells PostHog not to look up a location
privacy.crash.f.lib: says the report comes from Ocy
privacy.crash.f.platform: the operating system: Windows, Linux or macOS
privacy.crash.f.channel: where Ocy came from: the Microsoft Store, GitHub, Flathub, or the Linux or macOS download
privacy.crash.f.buildId: Windows only: identifies the exact Ocy build, so the places in the code can be read
privacy.crash.f.type: the kind of crash: an error in Ocy's code, or a Windows error code such as {code}
privacy.crash.f.value: the error message, with personal parts replaced (see below)
privacy.crash.f.mechanism: a standard field saying the crash was not caught
privacy.crash.f.frames: where in the code it happened: function names, file names inside Ocy's own code or a library it uses, line numbers, or positions inside the Ocy program file
privacy.crash.removedBody: Your username, computer name, home folder, Ocy's data folder and the names of games you marked silent are replaced with {user}, {host}, {home}, {data} and {game}. Any other full path from your PC becomes {path}.
privacy.crash.neverBody: Your settings, window titles, the programs or games you use, your IP address, your location, your name or account details.
privacy.crash.howBody: Over an encrypted HTTPS connection to {host}, and only after you press {send} for that report or chose {always}. If you're offline, Ocy waits and tries again about once an hour. Each report also carries Ocy's project key, a public, send-only key that cannot read any data.
privacy.crash.whereHeading: Where it goes and who sees it
privacy.crash.whereBody: PostHog, an analytics and error-tracking service, stores crash reports in its EU region. The connection's IP address is discarded instead of stored, and no location is looked up. Only damt.xyz, the developer of Ocy, can see the reports. They are kept for up to 2 years, then deleted automatically, and used only to find and fix bugs. They are never sold and never shared for advertising.
privacy.crash.pcReports: {file}: one file for each report that is waiting to be sent. At most 5 are kept (the oldest goes first), each at most 32 KB, and any report older than 30 days is deleted. If Ocy crashes several times in a row, only the first report is kept.
privacy.crash.pcNative: {file}: Windows only. A tiny raw record that a system-level crash leaves behind. At the next start Ocy turns it into a normal report and deletes it.
privacy.crash.pcState: {file}: only the number of reports sent today, for the limit of 5 a day.
privacy.crash.pcDeleted: A report file is deleted once it has been sent or declined. Choosing {never} deletes all waiting reports.
privacy.crash.offBody: Choose {never}. Nothing more is saved or sent, and reports that are waiting are deleted.
privacy.crash.deleteBody: Email {support} with the report ID. Copy it from {see} before you press {send}. We delete the report within about 4 weeks: PostHog removes events in weekly batches, and its backups expire about 2 weeks after that. Without the report ID, a report can't be linked to you, not even by us.
privacy.crash.separateBody: Crash reports and the usage stats each have their own choice. Turning one on or off never changes the other.
privacy.crash.storeBody: Windows itself may also send crash data to Microsoft through Windows Error Reporting, depending on your Windows privacy settings (Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback). That is Microsoft's system, not Ocy's. We see only a summary of it in Microsoft's developer dashboard.
privacy.crash.rightsBody: Ocy sends a crash report only with your consent ({send} or {always}), and you can withdraw it at any time by choosing {never}. You can ask what we hold for a report ID, ask us to delete it, and complain to your data protection authority. Contact: {support}
home.faq.13.a: Ocy saves a short report and, the next time it starts, asks whether to send it. Nothing personal is in it, and nothing is sent without your yes. {link} explains exactly what a report contains.
